author: Manuel Ibarra
headline: Business CFO & Transformation Leader | Strategic Finance | Business Management | Finance Executive | Capital & Performance Management | Prod
text:
The valuation side is what I’d watch. In a fund offering quarterly redemptions, NAV isn’t just a reporting number. It determines the price at which investors exit, with consequences for those who remain. When loans rarely trade, that price relies heavily on valuation judgment, often within ranges provided by third-party firms.

So the useful disclosure is specific: how much of the portfolio was independently valued this quarter rather than on rotation, where the marks sit within the provider’s range, and how often those valuations were overridden. In valuation control, a book consistently marked at the top of the range was a finding, even if every mark individually fell within it.

Redemption requests don’t necessarily mean credit quality is deteriorating. But they do increase the consequences of valuation uncertainty.

headline: Independent Legal Commentary | Not Affiliated With Any Law Firm or Attorney | For Discussion and Conversation Only
text:
Private equity just found a side door into law firms, and it does not require owning the firm.

An Arizona personal injury firm, Rafi Law Group, raised $125 million this year by moving its marketing, tech, and billing into a separate company and selling a stake in that. The operations arm was valued near $450 million. The lawyers still own the legal practice. The investors own everything around it.

This is the MSO model, and it is spreading. One firm that structures these deals reported closing more than 15 in six months, with about 100 more in the works.

The trade is real. Capital now, in exchange for a 20 to 30 year contract where someone else shapes your staffing and your tools.

If you were building your own firm, would you take the money?

The $55 Billion Power Play: Saudi Arabia’s Takeover of the Gaming Industry

Saudi Arabia is making one of the biggest investments in the history of the video game industry. Through its Public Investment Fund (PIF), the Kingdom is moving beyond esports sponsorships and gaming investments to gain control of major global entertainment companies. In September 2025, Saudi Arabia announced a $55 billion acquisition of Electronic Arts (EA), one of the world's largest video game publishers, alongside Silver Lake and Affinity Partners.

The deal valued EA at $55 billion, offering shareholders $210 per share. Financing included approximately $36 billion in equity and $20 billion in debt. PIF, which already owned 9.9% of EA, became the dominant shareholder, with an expected 93.4% ownership stake following completion.
This acquisition is part of Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 strategy to diversify its economy beyond oil and expand into technology, entertainment, tourism and digital media. Through PIF and its gaming subsidiary Savvy Games Group, the Kingdom has been building an international presence in game development, publishing and esports. Major projects, including the planned gaming district in Qiddiya, demonstrate the scale of its ambitions.

text:
In Saudi AI's newest financing deal, the power grid got a bigger cheque than the chips.

On 8 November, the National Infrastructure Fund (Infra) signed financing of up to SAR 2.5 billion (about $667m) with HUMAIN. Up to SAR 1.1 billion is for GPUs. Up to SAR 1.4 billion is for substations, transmission lines and grid connections for data centres built to support up to 1 GW. More of the money is going to electricity than to intelligence.

As our Group CEO Usman Ahmad put it this week, every technology wave is first an infrastructure story, then a data story, then an application story. The money follows the same order. It matches what we have seen in more than ten years of data work across the Kingdom.

Where we expect the next Saudi AI funding to go:

Power and cooling. The first bottleneck, and it is now being financed.

Data readiness. A ministry with 20 years of scanned files can't make use of a 1 GW campus until those files are searchable.

Vertical agents. Tools that do one job well, like claims checks for insurers or tender review for government buyers, built on local data and PDPL rules.

A word to founders: don't try to compete with HUMAIN on compute. Build the layer that makes that compute useful to a hospital, a bank or a municipality.

Which layer do you think gets funded next in the Kingdom?

author: Amr Ghonaim
headline: Demand Planning Manager | Sales Budgeting & Forecasting | Cost Management & Pricing | FMCG & Manufacturing | MBA Candidate | Power BI · Tabl
text:
Revenue growth isn't margin growth. Two Saudi food results this quarter show it.

→ Almarai reported Q3 2026 revenue of SAR 6.19 billion, up 11% year on year, while net profit rose about 1% to SAR 617.8 million (SPA, 5 October). The company credited a better revenue mix, mostly offset by higher dairy feed shipping costs and energy-driven distribution costs.
→ Savola's nine-month revenue grew 3.1% while net profit fell 22% to SAR 529.55 million (Argaam, 5 November). A large part of that drop came from one-off gains in last year's base, but its retail arm also reported margin pressure.

My take from a demand planning and commercial seat:

The cost that moves isn't always on the bill of materials. Freight, energy and distribution sit below gross margin, and they often get planned as a flat percentage of sales.

What I'd look at:
• Cost to serve by channel and region, refreshed whenever fuel or freight moves
• Mix targets in the S&OP plan, not only volume targets
• Separate targets for growth and for profit per case, so one can't hide the other

Top-line growth is good news. Margin per case tells you whether it's healthy growth.

Is your plan tracking profit per case, or only volume? 👇

— Amr Ghonaim | Demand Planning Manager

headline: Senior Accountant | Financial Analyst | Financial Reporting | IFRS | VAT & Zakat Compliance | Internal & External Audit | SAP Business One |
text:
A SAR 30 million swing from one price. 💡

Many Saudi groups think transfer pricing is a “multinational problem.” Since FY2024 it isn’t: Zakat payers, including wholly Saudi-owned groups, now fall under ZATCA’s TP bylaws.

→ Goods cost a Bahraini affiliate SAR 100
→ The market price is SAR 120
→ The group bills SAR 150 on 1,000,000 units
→ SAR 30M of profit leaves Saudi Arabia, and ZATCA can re-price, assess tax, and add penalties and WHT

What every finance and tax director should have on their radar:
✅ Arm’s length range: a 3.0% margin vs a 4.0%–7.1% range means an adjustment to the median
✅ TNMM does most of the work in regional audits of services and distribution
✅ Three-tier documentation: Master File, Local File and CbCR must tell one consistent story
✅ WHT can outweigh the mark-up: 20% on management fees, 15% on royalties, 5% on interest
✅ Reconcile three ways: the disclosure form, the financial statements, and the WHT returns
✅ Shifting margin to a 0% or 9% affiliate without substance is exactly what ZATCA challenges

Full policy brief in the slides. Swipe through 👉

Which of these is the biggest gap in your group right now: documentation, WHT characterisation, or benchmarking? Tell me in the comments.

Always verify current thresholds and rates with ZATCA and your tax adviser.
